source_document.body:
DoorDash has agreed to buy Instacart for about $17 billion, bringing the grocery delivery company and its retail technology business under the same owner as one of the largest restaurant delivery platforms.
What’s Related
The deal values Instacart at $65 per share, a 26% premium to its October 22 closing price, before reports of a possible sale. The deal will pay at least 75% of the purchase price in cash, with DoorDash shares accounting for no more than 25%.
The companies expect to close the acquisition in late 2027 or the first half of 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. They will continue to run separately until then, and DoorDash expects to retain Instacart’s brand, app, and tech products after closing.
The proposed combination would bring together Instacart’s grocery shopping technology and retailer relationships with DoorDash’s delivery and fulfillment services. Instacart works with more than 2,200 retail banners representing nearly 100,000 stores, and DoorDash says its customers could gain access to more than 50,000 additional stores.
RELATED STORIES: DoorDash Expands Into Retail Returns With $7.99 Pickup From Your Door | Online Grocery Takes Record 20.9% of U.S. Grocery Spending
DoorDash expanding its grocery role
DoorDash’s plans go beyond adding more grocery stores to its app. In its third-quarter earnings release, the company said managing grocers' inventory is an important part of improving delivery quality and reducing fulfillment costs.
Its DashMart Fulfillment Services business, launched in September 2025, already lets retailers sell products through DoorDash or their own channels while DoorDash handles inventory, picking, packing and delivery. Orders are filled from DashMart locations, rather than picked from a retailer’s store.
CVS Pharmacy and Party City were among the first retailers to use the service. DoorDash said the model lets merchants sell online without building their own fulfillment infrastructure.
DoorDash reported fulfillment accuracy above 99% for DashMart orders in the third quarter. It also said those orders arrived, on average, more than 10 minutes faster than other grocery orders in U.S. areas with an active DashMart location.
Those are company-reported results for its existing business. DoorDash expects Instacart’s order volume to help spread warehouse and inventory costs across more purchases.
What changes for shoppers
DoorDash said grocers would remain free to work with other delivery platforms after the acquisition. It also plans to let Instacart shoppers keep choosing grocery orders without having to accept DoorDash deliveries.
In a separate message to shoppers, Instacart CEO Chris Rogers said there are no immediate changes to how they accept or deliver orders. The companies see an opportunity to offer more orders closer to shoppers, but that remains an expected benefit of the combination.
DoorDash also plans to give DashPass and Instacart+ members access to both memberships for one fee. It estimates that would save members $100 million annually in combined membership fees.
Instacart continues to grow
The agreement comes as Instacart’s business continues to grow. The company reported 91.4 million third-quarter orders, up 10% from a year earlier, and revenue of about $1.1 billion, up 17%.
Advertising and other revenue increased 23% to $331 million. That business adds another revenue source alongside the fees Instacart earns from transactions.
DoorDash sees a multi-year path to at least $500 million in annual benefits from combining the businesses, after investments. It expects spending to exceed those benefits in the first year after closing, with positive net benefits starting in the second year.
For now, the acquisition remains subject to review. Required approvals include U.S. antitrust clearance, regulatory approvals in Canada and Israel, and a vote by Instacart shareholders.
